question: Have you worked in an organization experiencing explosive growth?
answer_summary: Honest gap admission: no classic Series A-B J-curve experience. Three related forms of growth strain: (1) Flint zero-to-one chaos — product, team, process, fundraising simultaneously under uncertainty. (2) DUG rapid scope expansion — Apple Vision Pro, Meta Quest+, Google Android XR while improving internal functions, lean team but complexity grew fast. (3) Observed people side of rapid growth going wrong — inconsistent onboarding, culture not reinforced, friction leading to attrition and layoffs. Understands tensions: speed vs quality, hiring vs absorption, expansion vs focus, process vs flexibility.
text:
I'll be honest: I have not been inside the classic Series A to B hypergrowth curve where headcount triples and the company is trying to scale everything at once. That is a real gap in my experience, and I would not want to overstate it.

What I have experienced, though, are a few related forms of growth strain.

First, at Flint, I experienced zero-to-one company building. That is a different kind of chaos. You are not scaling something that already works; you are trying to create product, team, process, and fundraising momentum at the same time, with limited resources and no real playbook. The pressure there is less about managing growth and more about making decisions under extreme uncertainty.

Second, at DUG, I experienced rapid expansion in scope, even if it was not textbook hypergrowth. In a relatively short period, we were pursuing new platform opportunities across Apple Vision Pro, Meta Quest+, and Google Android XR, while also trying to improve internal functions like HR, finance, legal, and customer support. The team itself stayed relatively lean, but the scope and complexity of what we were trying to handle grew very quickly. I saw how easily ambition can outpace structure when the organization has to absorb too much at once.

I have also seen the people side of rapid growth go wrong. I've been in situations where teams hired quickly, but the organization was not fully ready to absorb that growth well. Onboarding was inconsistent, culture was not reinforced clearly enough, people struggled to settle in, and over time that led to friction, attrition, and layoffs. That taught me that growth is not just about adding people or moving faster. It is about whether the organization has the structure, clarity, and cultural stability to absorb that growth without weakening itself.

So I would not claim that I have lived the exact Series A to B J-curve from the inside. But I do think I understand some of the underlying tensions quite well: speed versus quality, hiring versus absorption, expansion versus focus, and process versus flexibility. And I'm self-aware enough to know that this is still an area where I would have more to learn from people who have lived the classic version more directly.

question: What kind of person do you want to become in 10 years?
answer_summary: Three pillars for 10-year vision: (1) real insight — pattern recognition on why companies succeed/fail, which signals matter vs noise, (2) understanding founders deeply — reading people under pressure, judging founder-problem fit, resilience, followability, (3) genuinely useful after investment — through uncertainty, setbacks, turning points, earning 'they were there when it mattered' reputation. Judgment comes from proximity and market cycles, not frameworks. Mobile example: was a student observing from outside, wants to be in the room for next shifts. Does not picture a title first.
text:
In 10 years, I want to be someone founders call before they have even decided to start a company.

Not because I have the biggest brand or the loudest presence, but because they trust my judgment. To me, that means three things.

First, I want to become someone with real insight — someone founders trust to know what is likely to work and what is not. I want to develop the kind of pattern recognition that helps me understand why certain companies succeed, why others fail, how markets tend to respond, and which signals matter versus which are just noise. I want founders to feel that if they bring me an idea, I can help them see more clearly whether it has real potential or whether they are missing something important.

Second, I want to become very good at understanding founders. Not in a superficial way, but in a way that lets me see who this person really is under pressure. I want to get better at judging whether this is the right person for the problem, whether they have the depth, resilience, and clarity to keep building through difficulty, and whether they are someone others will genuinely want to follow. I think that ability to read people well is one of the hardest and most important parts of investing.

Third, I want to be the kind of investor who is genuinely useful after the investment. I do not just want to make a good decision at the beginning and then disappear. I want to help founders through the long process of building — especially through uncertainty, setbacks, and important turning points. I want to build the kind of reputation where founders say, "They were there when it mattered." That kind of trust takes years to earn and seconds to lose.

I do not think any of this comes from frameworks alone. It comes from staying close to companies, seeing decisions play out over years, and learning from both good outcomes and bad ones. It comes from experiencing real market cycles firsthand as an investor, not just as an observer. When mobile took off, I was a student. I saw that shift happen, but only from the outside. The next decade will have its own defining shifts, and I want to be in the room for those moments — making decisions, learning through them, and building judgment from the inside.

So when I think about 10 years from now, I do not picture a title first. I picture being someone with deep insight, strong judgment about people, and a reputation for being genuinely useful when it matters. That is the direction I want to grow into.

question: How did you build the due diligence evaluation system, and what does it do?
answer_summary: Built structured evaluation system for frontier tech ventures across Space, GenAI, Smart Agriculture at Changjo Architecture. Designed due diligence rubric from scratch — consistent scoring framework replacing gut feel. Built AI-powered dashboard using Gemini/Claude/ChatGPT for automated deep research, dual-rubric scoring, and multi-model investment committee debate. Produces structured company profiles for comparison. Built entirely from ground up.
text:
The CEO brought me back to Changjo Architecture in February 2026 specifically for strategy and market research — not the business development work I did in my first stint.

My main project has been building a structured evaluation system for frontier technology ventures across three sectors: Space, GenAI, and Smart Agriculture. I designed a due diligence rubric from scratch — a scoring framework that breaks down company assessment into consistent, comparable dimensions rather than relying on gut feel or ad hoc analysis.

On top of that, I built an AI-powered dashboard that automates much of the research and profiling process. It uses automated deep research via Gemini, Claude or ChatGPT to pull and synthesize information about target companies, applies dual-rubric scoring for structured assessment, and runs multi-model investment committee debate to stress-test conclusions from different angles. The output is a structured company profile that makes it easier to compare opportunities and identify where conviction is strongest.

I built the whole thing from the ground up — architecture, implementation, iteration. It directly reflects the kind of systematic evaluation work I want to do in VC: turning qualitative, fragmented information about early-stage companies into structured, defensible judgment.

question: Can you tell me more about the rubric?
answer_summary: Multi-agent AI pipeline for institutional-grade investment diligence on 100+ space companies. Two-stage funnel: Stage 1 scores across 12 dimensions heavily shaped by CEO's priorities, using multiple agents as advocates and skeptics. Stage 2 deep dive uses OSINT cross-referencing (USAspending.gov, SBIR.gov, SEC Form D, FCC/FAA filings, launch manifests, job postings) for syndicate mapping, TRL/MRL verification, unit economics, exit modeling. Unverifiable metrics flagged for founder Q&A.
text:
I built a multi-agent AI pipeline that runs investment diligence on over 100 space companies. It works in two stages — first a broad scoring pass to filter the universe, then deep research on the ones that survive.

In the first stage, every company gets scored across 12 dimensions. The scoring criteria were heavily shaped by what the CEO thought was most important — I calibrated the rubric around his priorities for deep-tech space investing, things like technology readiness, market position, capital efficiency, team integrity, exit realism, and so on. The pipeline uses multiple agents as advocates and skeptics, debating each company before producing a final score. That prevents any single model's bias from driving the output. The scores get bucketed into priority tiers and surfaced in a React dashboard.

For the companies that pass, stage two goes deeper — but not from company websites or PR. I cross-reference government contract databases like USAspending and SBIR, SEC Form D filings, FCC and FAA regulatory filings, launch manifests, even job postings. From there the system covers syndicate mapping, team background verification, independent TRL/MRL assessment against actual flight data, unit economics, and exit modeling that accounts for hardware CapEx dilution. Anything that can't be independently verified gets flagged for founder Q&A — no guessing, no hallucinating numbers.

question: How has the due diligence system changed an actual investment decision?
answer_summary: Biggest impact at screening/prioritization: side-by-side comparison across same dimensions replaced one-by-one intuition-based evaluation. Surfaced where moats were truly differentiated vs. only looked strong in isolation. Helped prioritize right deep dives. At deep-dive stage, OSINT research exposed two common weakness patterns: market demand gaps (claimed contracts but TAM couldn't support venture-scale returns) and technology readiness gaps (strong lab results but large gap to real-world deployment). Several companies dropped after deeper scrutiny.
text:
The biggest impact was at the screening and prioritization stage.

Once we scored the full universe on the same dimensions, we could compare companies side by side — especially within the same sector or sub-sector. That changed the process from evaluating companies one by one, largely from memory and intuition, to evaluating them relatively and systematically. It became much easier to see where a company's real strengths were, where its moat was truly differentiated, and where it only looked strong in isolation.

That mattered because it helped us prioritize the right deep dives. Instead of spending equal time on every interesting company, we could quickly identify which ones were genuinely worth the effort.

Then at the deep-dive stage, the system ran broader market research and OSINT — cross-referencing things like government contracts, filings, launch data, and hiring signals. That gave us a fuller picture not just of the company itself, but of the market quality, execution readiness, and whether the apparent strengths held up under scrutiny.

In several cases, companies that looked attractive in the initial scoring got dropped once the deeper research exposed weaknesses that weren't obvious at first glance. The most common patterns were:

- Market demand gaps — companies claimed strong contracts or customer pipelines, but the actual demand for their technology wasn't large enough to support venture-scale returns.
- Technology readiness gaps — companies had strong lab or pilot results, but the gap between controlled performance and real-world deployment was much larger than their materials suggested.

So the system didn't make the decision for us, but it changed where we spent time, what we eliminated early, and how quickly we reached conviction.

question: What are the limits of the due diligence system? When does it fail or mislead?
answer_summary: Three main limitations: (1) Public-data bias — system works best with visible companies, can confuse visibility with quality for stealth/early-stage companies. (2) Model reliability/hallucination — AI can produce credible-sounding false claims. Addressed through forced source/evidence chains, cross-referencing, recent data updates, but not fully solved. Unverifiable claims treated as leads, not truth. (3) Cannot judge founders — scores market/tech/credentials on paper but can't assess judgment, resilience, adaptability. System is a filter and time-saver, not a decision-maker.
text:
The biggest limitation is that the system is only as good as what it can see.

First, it has a public-data bias. It works well when a company leaves a real footprint — contracts, filings, hiring activity, investor disclosures, launch signals. But for very early-stage or stealth companies, there may be very little to work with. And even when data exists, it can be uneven: companies that are more visible can look stronger than quieter companies with better fundamentals. So one risk is confusing visibility with quality.

Second, model reliability is still a real issue. One of the biggest risks with AI-generated research is hallucination: claims that sound credible but are wrong — a contract that doesn't exist, a funding round that never happened, or a partnership that was misattributed.

I treated that as a core system design problem. So I forced the AI to provide sources, reasoning, and evidence chains rather than just outputs. I went through several iterations to make it back up factual claims, cross-reference them, and update them with the most recent available data instead of relying on stale summaries. That reduced the problem significantly.

But I still don't assume it's solved. If a claim can't be independently verified, I treat it as a lead to investigate, not as truth.

Third, it cannot judge founders. It can help score market, technology, and credentials on paper, but it cannot tell you whether a founder has judgment, resilience, or adaptability. That still requires direct conversation.

So I treat the system as a filter and a time-saver, not a decision-maker. It improves triage, helps structure comparison, and tells us where to look more carefully — but it doesn't replace human judgment.

question: How do you weight qualitative vs. quantitative signals for pre-revenue companies where most data is noisy?
answer_summary: Weights qualitative signals more heavily for pre-revenue — founder temperament is the operating system for everything. Uses quantitative as a discipline via three questions: is the moat claim falsifiable, do advantages compound, what evidence would change my mind. Acknowledges long VC experience creates an edge in founder reading that systems can't replicate. Qualitative first, quantitative as a check, humility about what takes experience.
text:
For pre-revenue companies, I weight qualitative signals more heavily, especially founder quality.

The reason is simple: in the first one to two years, most numbers are still noisy. What you really have is a small group of people making hundreds of decisions under uncertainty. So the founder's temperament becomes the operating system for everything — speed of iteration, product quality, hiring bar, culture, and how the company responds when reality breaks the plan.

That said, I don't ignore quantitative signals. I use them more as a discipline for thinking than as hard proof. I usually ask three questions:

1. Is the moat claim falsifiable, or is it just a story?
2. Are there any advantages that actually compound over time — through data, workflow, distribution, or usage?
3. What evidence in the next 12 to 24 months would change my mind?

That helps me separate real signal from narrative, even when the numbers are thin.

But the honest answer is that this is also where long investing experience matters most. I can build systems that structure market and technology analysis. I can reduce noise and make comparisons more rigorous. But reading a founder — their judgment under pressure, how they handle ambiguity, whether they can keep a team together when things get hard — that comes from years of sitting across from founders and seeing patterns repeat.

That's the part I most want to develop. So my answer is: qualitative first, quantitative as a check, and a lot of humility about what can only be learned through experience.

question: What patterns are you seeing in AI agent ecosystems, and why does it matter?
answer_summary: Researching AI agent ecosystems at Changjo. Core thesis: most companies overestimate model quality, underestimate interface and workflow ownership. Three patterns: (1) current chat interface is basically DOS — pushing work onto users, adoption breaks when behavior change is too high (Flint lesson), winners build invisible interfaces; (2) infrastructure value will commoditize, real question is who owns workflow layer — seat-based SaaS incumbents most at risk; (3) agent-to-agent economics via MCP/A2A protocols creating machine-to-machine layer with no historical precedent. Already built small-scale multi-agent coordination in DD dashboard.
text:
What I'm seeing is that the AI agent ecosystem is still very early, and most companies are overestimating the importance of model quality while underestimating the importance of interface and workflow ownership.

The first pattern is that most AI products still push too much work onto the user. The current chat interface is powerful, but in many cases it's basically a command line. It asks the user to become a prompt engineer instead of removing work for them. That matters because adoption usually breaks when behavior change is too high. I learned that very directly at Flint — we asked users to do too much upfront, and adoption stalled. I think many AI products today have the same risk. So I'm more interested in products where the interface becomes invisible and the agent just does the work.

The second pattern is around where value will settle. Right now a lot of value is concentrated in compute and infrastructure, which is normal in the early phase of a platform shift. But over time, those layers tend to commoditize. The more important question is who owns the workflow and the user relationship. That's why I think many seat-based SaaS incumbents are vulnerable: if an agent can execute the workflow directly, the GUI matters less and their pricing model gets pressured. So I'm watching for companies building durable advantages at the workflow layer — data, distribution, and lock-in.

The third pattern is the emergence of agent-to-agent coordination. With standards like MCP and A2A, agents are starting to discover tools, negotiate, and pass work across systems. That matters because it creates a new machine-to-machine layer where value may not sit in the same places it did in traditional software. At Changjo, I've built a small internal example of this using multi-agent debate to stress-test investment conclusions, and even at that scale you can see how coordination creates value beyond a single model response.

So the reason this matters is simple: the winners probably won't just be the companies with the best model. They'll be the ones that reduce user friction, own the workflow, and build durable position as agents start acting more autonomously.

question: How did you build a smart farm initiative from zero domain knowledge?
answer_summary: Joined Changjo Architecture late 2023 with colleague Joon to explore frontier tech expansion. No prior agriculture experience. Layered approach: studied CEA landscape and market sizing, visited 12+ indoor farm operators and food processing plants, consulted Professor Jeon at SNU for technical foundation (nutrient solutions, diagnosing tip burn). Built indoor farming rack systems, ran cultivation experiments, developed water-injection method that reduced water usage — Professor Jeon encouraged patenting. Initiative grew into dedicated Smart Farm division. Zero to new business line in ~5 months.
text:
When I joined Changjo Architecture in late 2023 with my colleague Joon, the CEO wanted to explore whether the company could expand beyond architecture into frontier technology ventures. Smart farming was one of the first areas we tested, and neither the company nor we had any real domain knowledge at the start.

So we approached it in layers. First, we built the knowledge base: we studied the CEA landscape, benchmarked competitors, sized the market, and tried to understand the economics of indoor farming. Then we went into the field. We visited more than a dozen indoor farm operators, spoke with founders about real bottlenecks like unit economics and scaling, and visited food processing plants to understand what happens after cultivation.

At the same time, we brought in outside expertise. We worked with Professor Jeon at Seoul National University, who helped us build the technical foundation — from nutrient solutions to diagnosing issues like tip burn in our own experiments. That helped us move from theory to real operating understanding.

Then we built and tested ourselves. We set up indoor farming rack systems, ran cultivation experiments, and compared different growing methods hands-on. Through that process, we developed a water-injection approach that reduced water usage in our tests compared with more conventional methods. When we showed it to Professor Jeon, he encouraged us to move quickly on patenting it.

The result was that the effort grew into a dedicated Smart Farm division inside Changjo Architecture that continued after we left. So in about five months, we went from zero domain knowledge to helping create a functioning new business line.

What I think this shows is that I can enter an unfamiliar domain, learn quickly, combine research with fieldwork, and turn ambiguity into something operational and commercially real.

question: How did you secure the Meta Quest+ deal and drive 55% revenue growth?
answer_summary: Assessed cannibalization risk of Meta Quest+ subscription model against existing paid sales, concluded incremental reach outweighed risk. Secured entry into the program. Redesigned promotions and DLC strategy (bi-monthly World Series Tour releases) to maximize recurring revenue. DLC revenue stabilized at ~25% of total. Combined effect: 55.47% YoY revenue growth in H1 2025.
text:
The 55.47% YoY revenue growth in H1 2025 came from a combination of strategic decisions, not a single win.

The biggest lever was securing entry into Meta Quest+, Meta's subscription program. The key challenge was cannibalization risk — if our game was available through a subscription, would it undercut our paid sales on the same platform? I ran the analysis and concluded that the incremental reach from Quest+'s subscriber base outweighed the cannibalization risk, especially since our title had already captured most of its organic audience on the Quest Store.

Once we were in Quest+, I redesigned our monetization approach. We launched a bi-monthly DLC release cadence — the World Series Tour — which created repeatable revenue drops and kept users engaged longer. DLC revenue stabilized at roughly 25% of total revenue, which gave us a recurring revenue layer on top of the subscription income.

I also restructured our promotion strategy to align with platform merchandising cycles, ensuring we had visibility during key sales periods.

The combined effect — Quest+ subscription revenue, DLC recurring revenue, and optimized promotions — drove the 55.47% growth. It wasn't about one big deal; it was about building a revenue engine with multiple reinforcing parts.

question: How did you initiate the Google Android XR partnership?
answer_summary: Leveraged existing Apple and Meta track record as credibility proof. Approached Google's XR team proactively when Android XR was still emerging. Secured dev kit access and negotiated upfront funding terms — unusual for a small studio. Managed cross-functional porting across engineering and business teams.
text:
The Google Android XR partnership was the third platform deal I built at DUG, and it came together because of a deliberate pattern I'd established with the previous two.

By the time Google was ramping up Android XR, we had already shipped on Meta Quest and Apple Vision Pro, with strong results on both — Quest+ entry, App Store Awards finalist. That track record became our credibility proof. When I approached Google's XR team, I didn't pitch from scratch; I pointed to delivered outcomes on competing platforms and argued that we were a proven partner who could ship on their platform quickly and at high quality.

The negotiation was focused on two things: dev kit access (critical for a small studio that couldn't afford to buy hardware at scale) and upfront funding terms to offset porting costs. Securing upfront payment is unusual for a studio our size, but I made the case based on our delivery track record and the strategic value of having a polished title ready for their platform launch.

I also managed the cross-functional porting process — coordinating between our engineering team on the technical port, the business side on contract terms, and Google's developer relations team on timeline and deliverables.

The broader lesson: each platform partnership made the next one easier. Apple credibility helped with Google. Meta revenue data helped with Apple. Building a track record is compounding leverage.

question: Tell me about the Meta funding deal you walked away from.
answer_summary: Meta offered a funding deal that had been previously dropped and renegotiated. After analyzing revenue-share vs. capital terms, concluded the deal would dilute the company's position and limit future fundraising leverage. Walked away to preserve equity and position the company for a stronger independent raise.
text:
This was one of the harder decisions at DUG because it meant saying no to real money on the table.

Meta had a funding program for studios building on Quest. We'd had an earlier version of the deal that fell through, and when it came back, the terms had changed. I renegotiated the structure, but when I analyzed the final terms — specifically the revenue-share implications versus the capital we'd receive — I concluded it wasn't a good deal for the company long-term.

The core issue was that the revenue-share terms would have effectively given Meta too much leverage over our economics on the platform. If we accepted, we'd be trading short-term capital for long-term margin compression. And strategically, taking that deal would have weakened our negotiating position for a future equity raise — investors would see the Meta revenue-share overhang as a liability.

So I recommended we walk away, and the CEO agreed. It wasn't a dramatic moment — it was a careful analysis of what the deal actually meant for the company's cap table and fundraising trajectory.

The lesson I took from it: not every deal that looks like money is actually good money. The discipline to say no when the terms don't serve the long-term interest is one of the most important things in business development — and in investing.

question: Tell me about your education at KAIST and KIT.
answer_summary: B.S. in Mechanical Engineering with Industrial Design double major at KAIST (National Scholarship, Dean's List, Cum Laude). M.S. in Mechanical Engineering at KAIST with National & BK21 Scholarship. Dual degree at KIT Germany (65 ECTS) during master's. text:

The education path might look unusual for someone in business development and VC, but each piece was deliberate. Engineering gave me the literacy to evaluate technical claims. Design gave me the instinct for user adoption. Research gave me the discipline to analyze systematically. And the international exposure — KAIST, KIT, living across Korea, Germany, Austria, and the US — shaped how I read people, markets, and opportunities across different contexts.

question: What is your technical background and what technologies do you work with?
answer_summary: Hands-on across multiple stacks: AI/ML (built a RAG pipeline with Pinecone, LLMs, worked with GNNs at Flint), distributed systems (Hadoop, Kubernetes at TmaxTibero), spatial computing (Unity, VisionOS at DUG), and full-stack web (Next.js, Python, TypeScript). question: What languages do you speak and how does your international experience shape your work?
answer_summary: Native bilingual in Korean and English. Advanced German (TestDAF 5/5/4/5). Lived in Korea, Germany, Austria, and the US. Cross-cultural perspective goes beyond language — understanding assumptions underneath communication, trust-building, and decision-making across different business cultures.

I'm a native bilingual in Korean and English, and I speak advanced German — I scored 5/5/4/5 on the TestDAF, which is the highest band in three of four sections.

For example, Korean business relationships often depend on demonstrating sincerity and long-term commitment before getting to the substance. American business culture tends to lead with the value proposition. German culture emphasizes precision and thorough preparation. At DUG, this mattered practically when I was working with Apple (US-headquartered but with a Korean Developer Relations team), Meta (US-based), and Google (US-based with Korean-market considerations). For VC, especially in a Korea-US cross-border context, this is a genuine differentiator. I can evaluate founders, build relationships, and support portfolio companies across both markets without the friction that comes from cultural misalignment.

question: What technical work did you do at TmaxTibero?

question: How do you lead and manage cross-functional teams?
answer_summary: Leadership approach shaped by operating as a bridge across stakeholders at every company. At TmaxTibero: coordinated customer, delivery, and engineering teams. At Flint: built decision culture across four co-founders using data. At DUG: managed partnerships across Apple, Meta, Google while coordinating internal engineering, legal, finance, and support functions.
text:
My leadership style is shaped by one consistent pattern: in every role, I've operated as a bridge between groups with different incentives, timelines, and languages.

At TmaxTibero, my daily work required coordinating three parties: customer expectations and timelines (Samsung, Hyundai), internal delivery team priorities, and the core DB engineering roadmap. You can't win that triangle with technical skill alone — you win by translating, making trade-offs explicit, and aligning incentives across groups that don't naturally communicate well.

At Flint, the challenge was different — leading among peers. With four co-founders, decision-making was hard at first. Too many meetings, too many votes. We solved it by building a data-driven decision culture: when we disagreed on product direction, we designed competing UIs and landing pages, released them publicly, and followed the data. That framework — 'disagree but commit, backed by evidence' — became our operating system.

At DUG, I was essentially a one-person business division managing external partnerships with Apple, Meta, and Google simultaneously, while also helping improve internal functions across HR, finance, legal, and customer support. The key was knowing when to go deep (critical deal negotiations) versus when to set up systems that could run without me (internal process improvements).

The common thread: I lead by making the implicit explicit — surfacing assumptions, clarifying decision rights, and converting disagreements into testable experiments rather than opinion battles. I've found that the best cross-functional leadership isn't about having authority over everyone; it's about being trusted by everyone because you translate fairly and deliver consistently.

question: Walk me through your resume.
answer_summary: Career arc framed as deliberate expansion from building technology to bringing it to market. Five phases: (1) KAIST/KIT foundation — systems + adoption + global mindset, (2) TmaxTibero — enterprise deployment reality, Samsung DBMS migration, (3) Flint — founding, seed funding, shutdown, learned tech-first mistake, (4) DUG — platform partnerships with Apple/Meta/Google, Vision Pro launch, App Store Awards finalist, distribution/timing as durable advantage, (5) Changjo — market research, diligence frameworks. Thread: compounding lenses (technical depth, enterprise adoption, founder reality, platform distribution) → VC as higher leverage role.
text:
If I summarize my career in one line: I've deliberately expanded from building technology to bringing it to market — and now I want to apply that operating pattern recognition as a VC.

First, the foundation. I double-majored in Mechanical Engineering and Industrial Design at KAIST because I was always interested in both sides: how systems work and why people actually adopt products. I also did research in Germany at KIT, which gave me a rigorous engineering mindset and comfort operating globally.

Then I learned enterprise reality at TmaxTibero. I started as an engineer on database infrastructure and worked on large enterprise deployments, including Samsung's DBMS migration. The key lesson was simple: in the real world, technology isn't judged by elegance — it's judged by deployment reality: risk, timelines, stakeholder alignment, and trust. That's where I learned how large organizations actually buy and adopt.

Then I became a founder at Flint. I co-founded an AI startup as COO, raised seed funding and government grants, built the product, navigated pivots — and we eventually shut it down. That experience permanently shaped my judgment. We made a common technical-founder mistake: starting from technology instead of a painful, urgent problem. I learned firsthand that great tech doesn't matter if the behavior loop doesn't stick, and I learned how to make decisions under uncertainty with real consequences.

After that I went to Devs United Games to scale. I joined as Director of Business to build the commercial and partnership side of an XR game studio. In about 18 months, I built platform partnerships with Apple, Meta, and Google — including launching on Vision Pro and becoming a finalist for the Apple App Store Awards, entering Meta Quest+, and closing a Google Android XR partnership. That chapter taught me how platform ecosystems work and how distribution and timing create durable advantage.

Most recently, I've been working with Changjo Architecture on new initiatives — market research and strategy across areas like smart agriculture and frontier tech — building diligence frameworks and evaluating companies.

The thread across all of this is that I've built a set of lenses that compound: technical depth, enterprise adoption, founder reality, and platform distribution. VC is the role where those lenses become higher leverage — I get to back great founders early, help them navigate hard decisions, and apply what I've learned across many companies rather than inside just one.

And that's why VC is the logical next step for me.

question: What's the strongest counterargument that AI agents are NOT a platform shift of PC/web/mobile magnitude?
answer_summary: Three counterarguments: (1) Trust gap may be structural — agent failures are probabilistic and non-repeatable, unlike deterministic software bugs. Without trust, users stay in the loop and agents stay as assistants. (2) Downstream economic problem — agents only justify higher pricing if they replace headcount, which requires trust first. Incumbents (Microsoft/Google) can bundle agents without standalone ROI pressure. (3) Regulatory — EU AI Act and FDA already impose human-oversight requirements on autonomous AI decisions. Conclusion: important software wave, not yet PC/web/mobile-scale platform reset.
text:
The strongest counterargument is that the trust gap may be structural, not just a timing problem.

Every previous platform shift had unreliable early phases — the web had broken pages and failed payments, mobile had crashes and spotty connectivity. But those were engineering problems with deterministic fixes. Agent failures are different. They're probabilistic. The same input can produce different outputs, and when an agent gets something wrong — a payment, a legal clause, a medical recommendation — the failure mode isn't repeatable. You can't just file a bug and patch it. That makes trust fundamentally harder to build, and without trust, users stay in the loop, and agents stay as assistants.

That trust gap creates a downstream economic problem. In theory, an agent that replaces a full employee is worth far more than a software seat — the buyer is saving on salary, not just on software. So the willingness to pay should be much higher. But that only works if the agent is reliable enough to actually replace the person. If trust isn't there, the human stays in the loop, the headcount doesn't shrink, and the agent becomes just another software cost that has to justify itself against existing tools. Meanwhile, incumbents like Microsoft and Google can bundle agent features into existing subscriptions without needing to prove standalone ROI — which makes it even harder for startups to compete on pricing.

The third is regulatory. The EU AI Act already classifies autonomous decision-making in hiring, lending, and medical diagnosis as high-risk, requiring human oversight by design. The FDA has separate approval pathways for AI that recommends versus AI that decides. If this pattern holds across industries, human-in-the-loop becomes a regulatory default, and agents stay as copilots regardless of how good the technology becomes.

So I still believe agents could become a platform shift, but I think there are at least three hard problems — trust, economics, and regulation — that need to be solved before this moves from an important software wave to a true computing reset. Until those gaps close, the default assumption should be: important software wave, not yet PC/web/mobile-scale platform reset.

question: You keep entering new domains every 1-2 years. How do you know you won't get restless in VC after the learning curve flattens?
answer_summary: Pattern is not restlessness but consistent attraction to entering unfamiliar territory and building judgment in ambiguity. VC is different because (1) learning curve never flattens — every deal is a new domain with deepening layers, (2) VC only becomes valuable if you stay — judgment compounds over full company cycles, sourcing compounds through founder referrals. VC attracts not for novelty but for compounding of judgment, relationships, and trust.
text:
That's a fair question, and I understand why my resume can look that way at first glance.

But I don't think the pattern is restlessness. I think the pattern is that I've consistently been drawn to the same kind of work: entering unfamiliar territory, learning quickly, and building judgment in ambiguous situations.

What I've learned about myself is that I stay most engaged when the problem keeps evolving. In roles where the scope became more defined, I felt like I was mainly applying what I already knew rather than developing new judgment. That taught me something important about the environment where I do my best work.

And that's exactly why VC feels different to me.

In VC, the learning curve doesn't flatten in the same way. Every deal is a new domain, and even within one domain, the deeper you go, the more layers appear — technology, market structure, founder psychology, regulation, distribution. The work stays intellectually alive.

But more importantly, VC only becomes truly valuable if you stay long enough for judgment to compound. The real learning comes from seeing full company cycles — how founders behave when things go wrong, how markets shift after the original thesis, how early signals actually play out over five to ten years. The same is true for sourcing and trust: the founders you help today become the people who refer the next generation of founders. That only works if you're consistent over time.

So for me, VC is not attractive because it gives me novelty. It's attractive because it gives me compounding — of judgment, relationships, and trust.

question: Of all your experiences, which one did you fail at most clearly, and what specifically did YOU get wrong?
answer_summary: Flint — three personal failures: (1) Avoided conflict with cofounders (close friends) when he believed in B2B knowledge retrieval direction — deferred instead of pushing, confusing conflict avoidance with collaboration. (2) Underused investors after raising — arrogant mindset, didn't communicate or ask for advice. (3) Shut down too early — confused friction with rejection, concluded thesis failed before fully exhausting iteration path. Lessons: push conviction early, use the people trying to help, diagnose carefully before quitting.
text:
Flint, clearly. And the failure was personal, not just circumstantial.

If I break it down honestly, I got three things wrong.

First, I avoided conflict when I should have pushed harder.
I believed we should move more toward B2B knowledge retrieval, but the team leaned another way, and I deferred. At the time, I told myself I was being collaborative. Looking back, I was avoiding conflict because we were close friends and I didn't want to be the person creating tension. That wasn't maturity — it was a lack of courage.

Second, I underused our investors after the round.
We worked hard to raise from strong people, and then once we had the money, we mostly put our heads down and built. Part of that was focus, but part of it was mindset. I overestimated the value of our internal conviction and underestimated the value of outside perspective. We didn't communicate enough, didn't ask for help, and didn't use the network we had earned access to. That was a mistake.

Third, I shut down too early.
This is the one I think about the most. The real mistake wasn't just that we stopped — it's that I concluded too quickly that the thesis had failed, when in reality we had not fully exhausted the iteration path. I confused friction with rejection, and I made that call before we had pushed far enough on simplification, positioning, and usability. That's on me.

What I took from that is very specific:

* if I have conviction, I need to push clearly and early;
* if people are trying to help, I need to use them;
* and if something isn't working, I need to diagnose more carefully before deciding it's dead.

Those lessons changed how I operate, and they're also part of how I evaluate founders now.
